In relation to the triad whose energeia each embodies, they stand, in terms of their mode of being, much as the “young men of love” stand to the “ladies of love” in Ramon Llull.

The three members of the first triad appear to the Shaykh al-Ishraq in their concrete imaginal reality as three brothers (Persian has no grammatical gender, and we need not be troubled by such distinctions in our own language here). Beauty contemplates himself and discovers himself to be the most precious of all treasures.

A great tenderness fills his being; he smiles, and thousands of angels come into existence, born from that smile. His younger brother, Love, also contemplates him. The sight of Beauty drives Love beside himself: he cannot turn away and remains in Beauty's service like a slave. Whenever he tries to break free and recover his independence, the youngest brother, Sorrow, seizes hold of him.

From Sorrow's embrace, which keeps Love forever longing for Beauty without fulfillment, Heaven and Earth were born and continue to endure. For this separation, this prohibition that places Beauty beyond Love's reach, is the secret not only of the gnostic's “story,” but of the whole human race and even the entire universe. Ruzbehan of Shiraz will take up the same theme (Book III, below).

Let us briefly follow the “story” as the Shaykh al-Ishraq tells it. Its first episode gives meaning to an “event in Heaven” familiar from the Qur'an and derived from an Old Testament apocryphon, the Life of Adam and Eve (Historia Adae et Evae): the command that the angels bow down before Adam. Suhrawardi tells it in a strikingly personal epic style. On learning of Adam's existence, Beauty mounts his glorious steed and rides toward the fortress, the Burg (shahrestân), in which Adam has come into being.

Love and Sorrow follow. Beauty takes complete possession of the human form, which thus becomes his mazhar, his supreme form of manifestation. Love catches up with him and is once more overwhelmed. Sorrow, his companion, lifts him to his feet. He sees all the beings of the heavenly world gathered around him to offer their submission, and all of them, from a great distance, kiss the earth at Beauty's threshold. This is the meaning of the mysterious Qur'anic verse: “All the angels bowed before him” (15:30).

A second episode opens with the “story” of Joseph, who in Islamic mystical literature traditionally represents the perfect revelation of Beauty. Love and Sorrow approach him, but he turns them away with sovereign indifference. The “story” of separation now begins. Each of the two younger brothers goes his own way, and each will reveal his secret to the chosen person who will embody it most fully among human beings.

Sorrow travels to the land of Canaan. Jacob sees him enter his place of prayer and recognizes in him the mark of love. Jacob questions him, and Sorrow reveals his secret: “I come from Nâkojâ-âbâd (the Land of No-Where, the land that cannot be seen anywhere by the senses, the Eighth Clime), from the City of the Pure.” Jacob becomes his inseparable companion: he is Sorrow.

Love makes his way to Egypt, where the story reveals the origin of the pair formed by Joseph and Zolaykha, the archetypal lovers of the Islamic mystical epic. Seeing Love pass by her place of prayer, Zolaykha asks him, “Where do you come from? What is your name?” Love answers: “I come from the land of the Spirit (Rûh-Abâd). Sorrow is always near the place where I dwell. I am a solitary Sufi, always setting out, in every direction.

“Each day I complete a stage of the journey; each night I stop somewhere to rest. In the darkness of exile I am called Love ('ishq). In my own kingdom I am called Mihr”—the Persian form of the name Mithra, meaning both “sun” and “love.” “In the heavens I am known as the Prime Mover; on earth I appear as a beggar. I have an ancient appearance, yet my youth is eternal. I possess no outward splendor, yet my ancestry is noble. Mine is a long story…”
Love then initiates Zolaykha into his secret.

First, where is his kingdom? A road of nine stages—the nine celestial Spheres—leads to it. Beyond the vault of the nine domes rises the fortress, the Burg, of the soul. For we know that one must emerge from the cosmic crypt to reach the Eighth Clime, Na-koja-abad, the “place” of the soul's castle, which lies beyond the coordinates of sensory space.
At this point the story describes the fortress in terms that reproduce, detail for detail, the description given in the “Epistle of the High Towers.”

The places and images are arranged here according to an architecture that illustrates Sohrawardî's vision of the theatrum mundi—the world as a theater—as perceived by the metaphysical imagination, whose sources and implications we discussed earlier.

At the heart, or on the summit, of this fortress lies the Spring of Life. Above this Burg, this fortified castle, rise other castles, just as in the “Tale of Exile” another Sinai rises above each Sinai.

Then comes the second part of the initiation, answering Zolaykhâ's question: “Why did Love leave his kingdom to come all the way here?” The answer develops the “story” of the “three brothers” briefly recounted above.
Zolaykhâ gives over her entire dwelling to Love. When Joseph appears, Love puts an arm around Zolaykhâ's shoulder, and together they move toward the contemplation that ends their separation.

Zolaykhâ is Love; Beauty and Love are reunited. Meanwhile Sorrow leads Jacob to Egypt, where he is to behold Joseph and Zolaykhâ—Beauty and Love—upon the throne. Then Sorrow, Jacob, and Jacob's sons, who had sold their Joseph, bow down.

And Joseph recites the verse: “O my father, here is the meaning of the dream I once told you: Father, I saw eleven stars, together with the sun and the moon; yes, I saw them bowing down before me in worship” (Qur'an 12:4). It is Beauty “in person” who speaks through Joseph's lips.
The final chapters (X–XIII) of the Vade-mecum, the handbook, return to the fundamental ideas and ethical demands of this religion of love for beauty.

Let us recall these lines in particular: “It is written: If God is beautiful, he must necessarily bring forth beauty. If everything that exists, whether bodily or spiritual, seeks perfection, you will likewise find no being that does not desire the beauty of forms.

“Reflect on this, then, carefully and deeply: Beauty is what haunts the desires of all beings; every effort is consumed in the longing to be united with her. Alas, how difficult it is to reach this Beauty, whom all desire! For union with her requires a mediator, and there is no mediator but Love.

“Yet Love does not welcome just anyone. He does not make his home wherever he happens to find himself; he does not reveal himself to every gaze. If someone comes to him, ready for such happiness, Love sends Sorrow, his faithful messenger, to cleanse the dwelling and make sure that no one but Love himself crosses its threshold” (chapter X).

We can now say this: Eros becomes sacred, is transformed into a sacrament of Love, precisely insofar as it is love of Beauty. For at the very beginning of all beginnings, Beauty herself is the revelation of the holiest of holies.

Wherever Beauty ceases to appear, wherever she is denied, desecrated, and blasphemed, Eros can no longer be transfigured; Eros himself has been caricatured, degraded, and profaned. The connection is a strict one, and certain things happening in our own day make us witnesses to it.

As the prologue to the Vade-mecum shows us, Love is essentially philokalia: love of Beauty. The name Philokalia, as we know, is also borne by a famous collection of ascetic writings in Eastern Christianity.

To avoid confusion, and recalling what we said at the beginning about “hieratic” (sacred) wisdom and art, we prefer to propose another word: hierokalia, or the sense of sacred Beauty—Beauty inseparably bound, in her very essence, to what is holy.

Without this hierokalia , there can be no religion of transfigured Eros. And such a religion is, by its nature, eschatological: it is concerned with the ultimate encounter that lies beyond earthly life.

Here we touch the deepest meaning of a conviction found in Zoroastrian faith: heavenly Beauty appears in the person of the angel Daênâ when the eschaton is reached, when the threshold of life after death has been crossed.

Yet the sudden appearance of absolute Beauty within earthly life is also eschatological. This happens, for example, when the mystery of Beauty is recognized as present in the beauty of another human being. Such an appearance can awaken in the one who sees it a love strong enough to break every attachment and every rule that binds us to earthly existence.

Of course, to recognize Beauty in this way, a person must already be straining with their whole being toward the vision awaited after death. The whole “story” of the gnostic now comes into play: the drama of separation from one's heavenly alter ego, one's other self.

The revelation of Beauty therefore brings that person to a breaking point, a “catastrophic” threshold, because it brings forward into the present what they had reason to expect only after death. This is what we mean by hierokalia, a word suggested to us both by Sohrawardî's Vade-mecum and by Rûzbehân's Jasmine of the Faithful of Love. It reaches infinitely further than what is commonly called, rightly or wrongly, “romantic” feeling.

In speaking of Beauty as an eschatological experience, we have just recalled the vision awaited after death by the Zoroastrian believer—a vision that also brings the gnostic's story to its conclusion. That reference was deliberate.
Throughout the mystical epic of Islamic Iran, this religion of transfigured Eros gives certain images inherited from Zoroastrianism a new power to transform the soul.

By changing them into symbols, it makes them imagines agentes: images that act upon us. This spiritual development accords so closely with the purpose of the shaykh al-Ishrâq, the Master of Illumination, who sought to renew the spiritual philosophy of ancient Iran, that we can best conclude with two examples.

The first comes from one of the greatest figures we have already encountered, Farîdoddîn ’Attâr (twelfth–thirteenth centuries). A poet of extraordinary and fertile genius, he created vast mystical poems in which the Iranian imagination gives brilliant expression to Goethe's words: “All that passes away is only a symbol.”

In a particularly daring ghazal, or lyric poem, ’Attâr cries out: “Whoever has lived in constant intimacy with the Temple of the Magi—what religious community could claim him? What ritual could bind him?—I stand beyond Good and Evil, beyond unbelief and religion, beyond theory and practice—for beyond all these, there are still many Stations .”
Certainly, to transgress the Law is still to acknowledge its existence.
Yet transgression of this kind brings a person to an extreme, eschatological threshold, and one's personal experience of ultimate things is not something to proclaim in the public square.
Consider how a master of Iranian Sufism, Shaykh Safîoddîn Ardabîlî (d. 735/1334)—the very man whom the Safavid dynasty regarded as its ancestor—explained this ghazal of ’Attâr to his disciples.

A fire altar is truly a “fire altar” when the sacred Flame burns there without ceasing. The Temple of the Magi and the fire altar signify the world of Love. Like the sacred Flame, love for the Divine Being never dies down.

For someone immersed in that love, what meaning could religious observances and rituals have if they were tainted by the impure desire to gain paradise? If such a person must outwardly observe them, or appears to observe them, it is with an inward sincerity that has made them wholly free for God.
Good and Evil, unbelief and religion, theory and practice: all these distinctions belong to the world of the rational intellect.
But in the world of Love, which lies beyond the very “place” of this world (see the discussion of Nâ-kojâ Abâd, the land of No-where, above), there are many Stations.

There are the Stations of detachment that frees one from material ties (tajrîd), and of solitude that makes one wholly oneself (tafrîd); the Stations of passionate love (’ishq) and loving affection (mahabbat); the Stations of renunciation (faqr), contemplative spiritual knowledge (ma’rifat), and unification that brings all into oneness (tawhîd).

None of this is contained in spaces already given or imposed upon us. Beyond all their boundaries, these Stations open up the realm of Love itself: the sanctuary where the sacred Flame is worshipped, the Temple of the Magi.

There the mystical lovers, the “Templars” of transfigured Eros, perform the service of Love. There is their qibla, the direction toward which they turn in prayer, and they have no other worship ... So the shaykh explained.

And in the two verses he recited during this “lesson,” we can still hear Iran's enduring longing for the heavenly Vision of light and love that it proclaimed to the world: “Our religion is the service of Love; our qibla is Love. Whoever has neither qibla nor Love—that one is the unbeliever.”
This ghazal belongs to a whole family of passionate declarations in the poetry of the great poet of Neyshâpûr, passages in which he uses a vocabulary drawn from Zoroastrian tradition.

Read with Safîoddîn Ardabîlî's commentary, the poem offers an ’irfânî, or mystical, interpretation of words inherited from Zoroastrianism. This spiritual phenomenon is closely related to Sohrawardî's Ishrâq, his philosophy of illumination; our friend Mohammad Mo’în once devoted an entire study to it .

Among its most powerful imagines agentes, or active images, is the “great master” or “prior” of the Magi (pîr-e Moghân). He is the Perfect Human Being, the heavenly Anthrôpos; he is the shaykh as spiritual guide (morshid), or, more directly, the Imam himself in Shiite gnosis.

The “priory of the Magi” is the world of the Divine Names. The “Magus” is the true witness to the One: the one who unifies and whom the One unifies. From here unfolds an entire constellation of symbols: the “sons of the Magi,” the “Temple of Fire,” the Môbed, the belt (kostî), and so on.

Towering over them all is the image of the “wine of the Magi,” together with the image of the Grail. Sohrawardî has given us ample reason to dwell on the Grail in these pages, and perhaps it is the key to this whole language of mystical interpretation .

It is from a setting dominated by this same vocabulary that we draw our second example. It comes from a vast nineteenth-century Persian mystical epic containing no fewer than seventy-six thousand couplets—roughly three times the length of Mawlânâ Rûmî's Mathnavî.
The poem is interwoven with prose passages and bears the title Kanz al-Asrâr (The Treasury of Esoteric Knowledge). This monumental work of Iranian Shiite Sufism unfolds in twelve books.

In Book XII we read: “An explanation of the Temple of Fire, which was nothing other than a visible form of the Divine Being's overpowering, exclusive, all-consuming Love. Zoroaster gave that Love a visible form and raised a fire altar to it.

“After the armies of Islam and the Arabs triumphed over Iran, this mystery was veiled from the Earth and withdrew into the innermost depths of the heart. Its emblem was taken up anew in the person of the royal princess (Shahrbânû, daughter of Yazdagard III), who became the mother of the Fourth Imam, Zayn ol-’Abidîn.

“Through her marriage at Yathrîb to the Prince of Martyrs (Imam Hosayn), she had entered the family of the Immaculate Ones. That is why this hadith, or saying, has been heard from the lips of the Prophet, prince of the Arabs and Persians: Never speak irreverently of Zoroaster, for Zoroaster was a messenger of the most loving Lord in Iran .”

This lengthy text, stated as a recurring theme, is then explained over some sixty couplets. It is not our task here to assess the historical accuracy of the tradition according to which the royal princess, daughter of Yazdagard III, the last Sasanian ruler of Iran, married the Third Shiite Imam, Imam Hosayn.

This tradition belongs to Shiite religious consciousness: to the understanding Iranian Shiism has of its own history, and to the form in which it expresses that understanding. As students of religious experience, we must therefore receive it as such, seeing—and helping others see—both what it explains and what it implies.

Whatever else may be said, the tradition reveals an event that has left an indelible mark on Iran's religious consciousness. Its representation of that event is the keystone that holds together the architecture of Iran's spiritual universe.
Notice, in this connection, the importance of women in Shiite sacred imagery. Fâtima the Radiant is the link between the Prophet and the Twelve Imams.

The royal princess, daughter of Yazdagard III, establishes continuity between Zoroastrian Iran and Shiite Iran: between the religion of love symbolized by the flame upon the fire altar and the religion of love affirmed in the walâyat, the spiritual bond of devotion and guardianship centered on the Imams.
As for the text of the tradition, preserved and elaborated by a nineteenth-century Iranian Sufi, we cannot at present identify its source.
But the shaykh al-Ishrâq would surely have embraced it, so clearly does it support the conviction with which he undertook the great project of his life.

The long procession of Iranian mystics, headed by figures such as Sanâ’î, Sohrawardî, and ’Attâr, continues into the nineteenth-century Shiite Sufis. That is why their testimony seems to us the most fitting conclusion to the first two books of this work, devoted respectively to Shiism and to the shaykh al-Ishrâq.

Of Sohrawardî himself, let us say in closing that, for all its greatness, his work may appear to have been left unfinished, cut short by his martyrdom while he was still young. His book of “Eastern Theosophy”—The Philosophy of Illumination—is a great book in its ambition; in length and style, however, it is closer to a concise compendium.

Had he lived, its author would surely have expanded the outlines hastily set down on paper during his travels. Even as it stands, his work has left its mark on Iranian thought for eight centuries. It has never ceased to live in the minds of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, whether their earthly home was Iran or India.

But we should not imagine that life in this world was ever easy for them. All of them, even in the Safavid period, endured harassment. These members of the “family of Ishrâq” were solitary souls, hermits of the heart, exiles who heard “the call from the right-hand side of the valley, from within a bush” (Qur'an 28:30): the call from the “East” that rises at the heart of the “Tale of Exile.”
To call a person home from exile, that call must first awaken the exile to the knowledge that they are an exile. And in the noise and tumult of this world, nothing is more difficult.

More than once we have quoted the invocation from a psalm of Sohrawardî: “Deliver the people of Light; lead Light toward Light.” It echoes the faith of those who know that “the Darkness did not receive the Light” (John 1:5).
And it echoes the faith of those who know that the pure Islam of the true believers “began as a stranger (gharîb) and will become a stranger again, as it was in the beginning.

“Blessed are those who become strangers!” This famous saying of Imam Ja’far gives its full meaning to a devotion to the Shiite cause that reaches beyond every horizon of this world. It speaks to all the “strangers” who dare to accept the challenge: to go into exile from exile itself. It speaks above all to Salmân the Persian and to everyone for whom he stands.

And the shaykh al-Ishrâq, more than anyone, deserves to lead the procession of pilgrims who come in spirit to Salmân the Persian's tomb, there to repeat: “May I live and die, loyal friend, as you did ... you who never betrayed .”
